name: desmoplastic small round cell tumour
aliases: intra-abdominal desmoplastic small round cell tumour

reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
clinicalPearls: A rare, highly aggressive small round blue cell sarcoma with a striking predilection for adolescent and young adult males, typically arising on peritoneal and other serosal surfaces.
Defined by the recurrent EWSR1-WT1 gene fusion, which produces a chimeric transcription factor detectable by molecular testing and is essentially pathognomonic.
Presents with abdominal or pelvic pain, distension and often multiple bulky peritoneal masses without an identifiable organ of origin at diagnosis.
Histology shows nests of small round cells embedded in a prominent desmoplastic stroma, with characteristic polyphenotypic differentiation.
Immunohistochemistry shows co-expression of epithelial (cytokeratin, EMA), mesenchymal (desmin in a dot-like pattern) and neural markers, reflecting divergent differentiation.
Disease is usually widely disseminated across the peritoneum at presentation, frequently with hepatic, nodal and, later, pulmonary spread.
Management is multimodal, combining intensive chemotherapy, aggressive cytoreductive surgery and radiotherapy, often coordinated in sarcoma reference centres.
Despite aggressive treatment the disease is prone to relapse, and outcomes remain among the poorest of the small round cell sarcomas.
reference.pathophysiology: Desmoplastic small round cell tumour is driven by a balanced chromosomal translocation that fuses the EWSR1 gene with the Wilms tumour gene WT1, generating a chimeric protein in which the transcriptional activation domain of EWSR1 is joined to the DNA-binding zinc-finger domain of WT1. This aberrant transcription factor dysregulates target genes, including those encoding growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor, which is thought to drive the intense desmoplastic stromal reaction that characterises the tumour. The fusion product also promotes a polyphenotypic programme, explaining the simultaneous epithelial, mesenchymal and neural marker expression. The tumour has a marked tropism for mesothelial-lined surfaces, spreading diffusely across the peritoneum as multiple implants rather than a single dominant mass, which underlies its typical widespread intra-abdominal presentation and difficulty in achieving durable control.
additionalDifferentials: Ewing sarcoma and other EWSR1-rearranged sarcomas
small cell carcinoma metastatic to the abdomen
poorly differentiated carcinomatosis of unknown primary
additionalInvestigations: contrast-enhanced CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis for disease mapping
MRI of the pelvis for local extent
core or surgical biopsy with comprehensive immunohistochemical panel
molecular detection of the EWSR1-WT1 fusion by FISH or RT-PCR
FDG-PET for staging and response evaluation
diagnostic laparoscopy to assess peritoneal disease burden
baseline organ-function and fertility-preservation assessment before intensive therapy
redFlags: rapidly enlarging abdominal mass with pain in a young male
malignant ascites or bowel obstruction from peritoneal disease
hepatic or pulmonary lesions indicating distant spread
ureteric obstruction or hydronephrosis from pelvic bulk
constitutional decline with weight loss and cachexia
reference.prognosis: Desmoplastic small round cell tumour carries a poor prognosis, with frequent relapse and low long-term survival even after intensive multimodal therapy. The best outcomes are seen when complete or near-complete cytoreduction can be achieved in the context of systemic treatment.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for Ewing sarcoma when only EWSR1 rearrangement is demonstrated without confirming the WT1 partner.
Attributing widespread peritoneal disease to carcinomatosis and omitting fusion testing in a young patient.
Overlooking the characteristic dot-like desmin staining that supports the diagnosis.
Assuming resectability without full imaging of the extent of peritoneal and extraperitoneal spread.
Delaying referral to a sarcoma centre, compromising access to coordinated multimodal treatment.
